before: I discovered that a student needing shelter can obtain it for a lifetime for no more than he currently pays in annual rent. If my boasting seems excessive, my excuse is that I boast for humanity, not merely myself; my own faults and inconsistencies do not alter my statement’s truth. Despite much cant and hypocrisy—chaff I struggle to separate from my wheat, and regret as much as anyone—I will breathe freely and stretch myself in this matter. It relieves both body and moral nature, and I refuse to become the devil’s advocate through humility. I shall try to speak well of truth. At Cambridge College, simply renting a room a little larger than mine costs thirty dollars yearly, though the corporation built thirty-two together beneath one roof. The student also endures numerous noisy neighbors and possibly a fourth-floor room. I cannot help thinking that if we possessed more genuine wisdom in these respects, we would need less education precisely because we would already have acquired a greater amount of it; and the financial expense of obtaining an education would to a very considerable degree disappear altogether. Conveniences at Cambridge or elsewhere cost the student or another person ten times as much life as proper management by both parties would require. The highest-priced things are never what the student needs most. Tuition, for example, occupies a large place in the term’s bill; the much more valuable education obtained among the most cultivated people of his generation costs nothing. Colleges are generally founded by collecting dollars and cents, then blindly carrying the division of labor to its extreme—a principle always requiring caution. A contractor is brought in to speculate on the undertaking; he hires Irishmen or other workers actually to lay the foundations, while prospective students supposedly prepare themselves for college. Successive generations pay for these oversights. I think it would be _better_ for students, or those hoping to benefit, even to lay the foundations themselves. A student who secures prized leisure and seclusion by systematically avoiding necessary human labor gets an ignoble, unprofitable leisure. He cheats himself of the experience that alone makes it fruitful. “But,” someone says, “you do not mean that students should work with their hands instead of their heads?” Not exactly, though he might think my meaning much the same. They ought not merely _play_ at life or _study_ it while the community pays for this costly game. They should seriously _live_ it from beginning to end. How could young people learn living better than by trying the experiment immediately? Surely it would exercise their minds as much as mathematics. To teach a boy arts and sciences, for example, I would not follow the usual practice of merely sending him near a professor, where everything except the art of living is taught and practiced. There he surveys the world through telescopes and microscopes, never his unaided eye; studies chemistry without learning how bread is made, mechanics without learning how it is earned; discovers Neptune’s new satellites without noticing specks in his own eyes or the vagabond around whom he himself revolves. He contemplates monsters in a drop of vinegar while surrounding monsters devour him. Who would advance further in a month: the boy making a pocketknife from ore he dug and smelted, reading what the task required, or the boy attending metallurgy lectures at the Institute and receiving a Rodgers’ penknife from his father? Which is likelier to cut his fingers?... Imagine my astonishment on leaving college when told I had studied navigation! A single trip down the harbor would have taught me more. Even the _poor_ student learns only _political_ economy; our colleges do not even sincerely profess that economy of living synonymous with philosophy. While reading Adam Smith, Ricardo, and Say, he consequently plunges his father hopelessly into debt.

before: However incidental and therefore uninformative these figures may seem, their completeness gives them some value. I received nothing without accounting for it in some way. The calculation shows that food alone cost me about twenty-seven cents weekly in cash. For nearly two years afterward my diet was unleavened rye and Indian meal, potatoes, rice, very little salt pork, molasses, and salt; I drank water. Living chiefly on rice suited someone so fond of India’s philosophy. To answer habitual faultfinders, I should add that I sometimes dined out, as I always had and hope to have opportunities to do again. Often this disrupted my household arrangements. But since dining out was a constant element, as I have said, it does not affect a comparison of this kind at all.

before: At first I made bread from Indian meal and salt alone, genuine hoe-cakes baked before my outdoor fire on a shingle or on the end of timber cut off while building. They often acquired smoke and a pine flavor. I also tried flour, but eventually found rye mixed with Indian meal the pleasantest and most convenient. In cold weather baking several small loaves in succession amused me considerably; I tended and turned them as carefully as an Egyptian watching hatching eggs. These were true cereal fruits ripening under my care, with a fragrance to my senses like other noble fruits’. I wrapped them in cloth to preserve it as long as possible. I studied the ancient, indispensable craft of breadmaking, consulting whatever authorities I found. My studies began with the first unleavened bread, when people passed from the wildness of nuts and meats to this milder, more refined food. Then I followed the dough’s accidental souring, supposedly the discovery of leavening, and subsequent fermentations, down to “good, sweet, wholesome bread,” the staff of life. Some regard leaven as bread’s soul, the _spiritus_ filling its cellular structure, preserved religiously like the Vestal fire. I suppose a precious bottle brought on the Mayflower began America’s supply, its influence still rising, swelling, and spreading in waves of grain across the country. Faithfully I fetched this seed from the village until one morning I forgot the rules and scalded my yeast. The accident taught me that even yeast was unnecessary: I made discoveries by analysis, not synthesis. Ever since I have happily omitted it, although most housewives earnestly insisted that safe, wholesome bread without yeast was impossible, and elderly people predicted my vital powers would quickly decline. I find it no essential ingredient; after a year without it I remain among the living. I am glad to avoid the petty business of carrying a bottle in my pocket that sometimes popped and discharged its contents to my embarrassment. Leaving it out is simpler and more respectable. Humanity adapts to climates and circumstances better than almost any animal. Nor did I add sal soda or any other acid or alkali. Apparently my bread followed Marcus Porcius Cato’s recipe from about two centuries before Christ: “Panem depsticium sic facito. Manus mortariumque bene lavato. Farinam in mortarium indito, aquæ paulatim addito, subigitoque pulchre. Ubi bene subegeris, defingito, coquitoque sub testu.” I understand this as: “Make kneaded bread this way. Wash your hands and trough thoroughly. Put meal in the trough, gradually add water, and knead thoroughly. Once it is well kneaded, shape it and bake beneath a cover”—in other words, a baking kettle. Not a word of leaven. But I did not always use this staff of life. Once my empty purse kept all bread from my sight for more than a month.

Having flown across the Green Mountains and the Connecticut, it shoots like an arrow through the township in ten minutes, almost unseen by other eyes. It travels onward.

before: When I stayed late in town, how pleasant it was to launch myself into the night, especially a dark, stormy one. With a sack of rye or Indian meal on my shoulder, I would set sail from some bright village parlor or lecture room toward my snug woodland harbor. Having made everything secure on deck, I withdrew below with a merry crew of thoughts, leaving only my outward self at the helm, or even lashing the helm in place when the sailing was easy. Many a cheerful thought came to me beside the cabin fire “as I sailed.” No weather ever wrecked or seriously troubled me, although I met some fierce storms. Even on an ordinary night, the woods are darker than most people imagine. Often I had to look up at the strip of sky between the trees above the path to find my way. Where no cart track existed, my feet felt out the faint trail I had worn, or my hands touched particular trees whose positions I knew, letting me steer between them. Thus I would always pass between two pines in the middle of the woods, scarcely eighteen inches apart, on the darkest night. Sometimes, arriving home late on a dark, damp night, I could not remember a single step of the journey. My feet had followed the path my eyes could not see while I dreamed and wandered in my thoughts, until raising my hand to lift the latch woke me. I thought perhaps my body could find its own way home if its master abandoned it, just as a hand finds the mouth unaided. Several times, when a visitor stayed into the evening and the night turned dark, I had to lead him to the cart track behind my house and point out his direction, telling him to trust his feet more than his eyes in keeping to it. On one particularly dark night I sent two young men on their way like this after they had been fishing in the pond. They lived about a mile away through the woods and knew the route perfectly well. A day or two later, one told me they had wandered near their own home for most of the night and arrived only toward morning. Several heavy showers had fallen meanwhile; the leaves were drenched, and so were they, right through to their skin. I have heard of many people losing their way even in the village streets when the darkness was, as the saying goes, thick enough to cut with a knife. People from the outskirts who had driven their wagons into town to shop have had to stay overnight. Gentlemen and ladies making a social call have strayed half a mile, feeling the sidewalk only with their feet and failing to notice when they turned. Getting lost in the woods at any time is a surprising, memorable, and valuable experience. Even in daylight, during a snowstorm, you may come onto a familiar road and be unable to tell which direction leads to the village. You know you have traveled it a thousand times, yet recognize nothing; it seems as strange as a road in Siberia. At night, of course, the confusion is infinitely greater. On even our most ordinary walks we unconsciously steer like pilots, using familiar beacons and headlands. If we stray beyond our usual course, we still hold in mind the bearing of some nearby cape. Only when we are utterly lost or turned around do we appreciate Nature’s vastness and strangeness—and in this world, a man need only be turned around once with his eyes shut to lose his way. Every time we wake, whether from sleep or from absorption in thought, we must learn the compass points again. Only after we lose our way—after we lose the world, that is—do we begin to find ourselves, to understand where we stand and how infinitely far our connections extend.

before: The pond gave me a well already dug. For four months each year its water is as cold as it is always pure; then, I think, it equals any water in town, if it is not the best. In winter, water open to the air is colder than springs and wells sheltered from it. On March 6, 1846, pond water that had stood in my room from five the previous afternoon until noon measured 42°. The room had sometimes reached 65° or 70°, partly from sunshine on the roof. Yet the water was still one degree colder than water freshly drawn from one of the village’s coldest wells. That day the Boiling Spring measured 45°, warmest of all I tested, although in summer it is the coldest I know; in summer, too, shallow stagnant surface water does not mix with it. Walden’s depth also keeps it from becoming as warm in summer as most sun-exposed water. In the hottest weather I generally put a pailful in my cellar, where it cooled overnight and stayed cool all day, although I also used a nearby spring. After a week it was as good as when dipped, without any pump flavor. Anyone camping for a summer week beside a pond need only bury a pail of water several feet down in the camp’s shade to dispense with the luxury of ice.

before: The north wind had already started cooling the pond, though its depth required many weeks of steady blowing. When I began lighting evening fires, before plastering the house, the many gaps between the boards made the chimney draw particularly well. Yet I spent happy evenings in that cool, airy room, surrounded by rough brown knotty boards, with bark-covered rafters high above. The house never looked so pleasing after I plastered it, though I had to admit it was more comfortable. Shouldn’t every room people live in be high enough to allow some darkness overhead, where evening shadows can flicker among the rafters? Such shapes please fancy and imagination more than frescoes or the costliest furnishings. I might say I only began truly inhabiting my house when I used it for warmth as well as shelter. I had acquired two old fire-dogs to lift the wood off the hearth. Seeing soot gather at the back of my own chimney did me good, and I stirred the fire with unusual satisfaction and a greater right to do so. My dwelling could barely accommodate an echo, so small was it. But having just one room and distant neighbors made it seem larger. Every attraction of a house was gathered into that room: kitchen, bedroom, parlor, and family room. Whatever pleasure a house offers parent or child, master or servant, I enjoyed it all. Cato says a family’s master (_patremfamilias_) must have in his country villa “cellam oleariam, vinariam, dolia multa, uti lubeat caritatem expectare, et rei, et virtuti, et gloriæ erit,” meaning “an oil and wine cellar, many casks, so that it may be pleasant to expect hard times; it will be for his advantage, and virtue, and glory.” My cellar held a firkin of potatoes and about two quarts of peas containing weevils; my shelf held a little rice, a molasses jug, and a peck each of rye and Indian meal.

before: Today only hollows in the earth mark these homes, with buried cellar stones and sunny grass bearing strawberries, raspberries, thimble-berries, hazel-bushes, and sumachs. A pitch-pine or twisted oak stands in the former chimney corner; perhaps a fragrant black-birch waves over the old doorstep. Sometimes you can see the well’s hollow, once fed by an oozing spring, now dry and tearless grass. Or the last of the family covered it deep under the turf with a flat stone, to be discovered only in some distant future. Covering wells must be such a sorrowful act! It happens as wells of tears open. Like abandoned fox burrows, these old cellar hollows are all that survives where human life once bustled and people debated “fate, free-will, foreknowledge absolute” in one form or dialect after another. All I can discover of their conclusions is that “Cato and Brister pulled wool,” about as enlightening as histories of better-known philosophical schools.

before: Ice-cutters usually hasten a pond’s breakup by opening large areas: wind-stirred water erodes the surrounding ice even in cold weather. Walden did not respond that way that year, however; she soon put on a thick new garment in place of the old. This pond opens later than every other pond in the neighborhood, partly because her water is much deeper and partly because no stream runs through her to melt the ice or wear it away. I have never known her to open during winter, even in ’52–3, which severely tested the ponds. She generally opens around April first, a week or ten days after Flint’s Pond and Fair-Haven. Melting begins on the north side and in the shallows where freezing began. Less affected by brief temperature changes, she marks the season’s real progress better than any nearby water. A few severely cold March days may greatly delay those other ponds’ opening, while Walden’s temperature rises almost without interruption. On March 6th, 1847, a thermometer placed in Walden’s middle read 32°, the freezing point; near shore it read 33°. That same day, in Flint’s Pond’s middle it showed 32½°, but in shallow water a dozen rods offshore, beneath a foot of ice, 36°. That three-and-a-half-degree difference between Flint’s deep and shallow water, together with its large proportion of shallows, explains its much earlier opening. Its shallowest ice was then several inches thinner than its central ice. In midwinter the centre had been warmest, with the thinnest ice. Anyone wading a pond’s shores in summer likewise notices how much warmer water is close to shore, only three or four inches deep, than a little further out, and how much warmer deep water is at the surface than near the bottom. In spring the sun does more than raise air and ground temperatures. Its heat passes through ice a foot or more thick and reflects from the shallow bottom, warming the water and melting the ice underneath while directly melting the upper surface. This makes it uneven and stretches its air bubbles upward and downward until the whole is honeycombed, finally vanishing suddenly in one spring rain. Ice, like wood, has a grain. When a block starts rotting or “combing,” taking on a honeycomb appearance, its air cells always stand at right angles to the former water surface, whatever the block’s position. Above a rock or log close to the surface, the ice is much thinner and often melts entirely through this reflected warmth. I am told that Cambridge’s experiment in freezing water in a shallow wooden pond allowed cold air underneath, exposing both sides, yet sunshine reflected from its bottom more than cancelled that advantage. When warm midwinter rain removes Walden’s snow-ice and leaves hard, dark or transparent ice in the middle, a band of rotten white ice, thicker though it is, remains around shore, a rod or more wide, produced by this reflected heat. after: Ice-cutters usually hasten a pond’s breakup by opening large areas: wind-stirred water erodes the surrounding ice even in cold weather. Walden did not respond that way that year, however; she soon put on a thick new garment in place of the old. This pond opens later than every other pond in the neighborhood, partly because her water is much deeper and partly because no stream runs through her to melt the ice or wear it away. I have never known her to open during winter, even in ’52–3, which severely tested the ponds. She generally opens around April first, a week or ten days after Flint’s Pond and Fair-Haven. Melting begins on the north side and in the shallows where freezing began. Less affected by brief temperature changes, she marks the season’s real progress better than any nearby water. A few severely cold March days may greatly delay those other ponds’ opening, while Walden’s temperature rises almost without interruption. On March 6th, 1847, a thermometer placed in Walden’s middle read 32°F, the freezing point; near shore it read 33°. That same day, in Flint’s Pond’s middle it showed 32½°, but in shallow water a dozen rods offshore, beneath a foot of ice, 36°. That three-and-a-half-degree difference between Flint’s deep and shallow water, together with its large proportion of shallows, explains its much earlier opening. Its shallowest ice was then several inches thinner than its central ice. In midwinter the centre had been warmest, with the thinnest ice. Anyone wading a pond’s shores in summer likewise notices how much warmer water is close to shore, only three or four inches deep, than a little further out, and how much warmer deep water is at the surface than near the bottom. In spring the sun does more than raise air and ground temperatures. Its heat passes through ice a foot or more thick and reflects from the shallow bottom, warming the water and melting the ice underneath while directly melting the upper surface. This makes it uneven and stretches its air bubbles upward and downward until the whole is honeycombed, finally vanishing suddenly in one spring rain. Ice, like wood, has a grain. When a block starts rotting or “combing,” taking on a honeycomb appearance, its air cells always stand at right angles to the former water surface, whatever the block’s position. Above a rock or log close to the surface, the ice is much thinner and often melts entirely through this reflected warmth. When warm midwinter rain removes Walden’s snow-ice and leaves hard, dark or transparent ice in the middle, a band of rotten white ice, thicker though it is, remains around shore, a rod or more wide, produced by this reflected heat. As I have also said, bubbles inside the ice act as burning-glasses, melting the ice below.

before: Sometimes, in a single spring day, this sandy eruption or foliage blankets a bank twenty to forty feet high for a quarter-mile along one or both sides. Its sudden emergence makes these sand leaves remarkable. Seeing the lifeless bank on one side—the sun reaches one side first—and on the other this lush growth made within an hour, I feel I have entered the laboratory of the Artist who made the world and me. Here he still works, playing on the bank, scattering fresh designs in a surplus of energy. I seem closer to the globe’s vital organs, for this overflow resembles the leafy mass of an animal’s entrails. Sand itself anticipates the plant leaf. No wonder earth expresses herself outwardly through leaves: inwardly she labors so intensely with the idea. Her atoms already know this law and are pregnant with it. The overhanging leaf can see its prototype below. _Inside_ globe or animal, the form is a moist, thick _lobe_, a word especially fitting liver, lungs, and _leaves_ of fat (?e?ß?, _labor_, _lapsus_, flowing or slipping down, a lapsing; ??ß??, _globus_, lobe, globe; also lap, flap, and many other words). _Outside_ it is a dry, thin _leaf_, just as _f_ and _v_ are pressed, dried forms of _b_. The root letters of _lobe_ are _lb_: the soft mass of _b_—one lobe, or B with two—with liquid _l_ behind, pushing it forward. In globe, _glb_, the throaty _g_ adds the throat’s capacity to the meaning. Birds’ feathers and wings are thinner, drier leaves still. Similarly, the earth’s lumpish grub becomes an airy, fluttering butterfly. The globe itself continually surpasses and transforms itself, taking wings in its orbit. Even ice starts in delicate crystal leaves, as though poured into moulds left by water plants’ fronds on the watery mirror. An entire tree is only one leaf; rivers are larger leaves still, their pulp the earth between them, their axils holding towns and cities like insect eggs.

before: We ought to look more often over our vessel’s stern rail like curious passengers, instead of travelling like dull sailors picking oakum. The globe’s far side is simply where our correspondent lives. Our voyages merely follow great circles, and doctors treat only skin complaints. Someone rushes to Southern Africa to hunt giraffes; surely that cannot be his true quarry. How long would anyone chase giraffes if free to do so? Snipe and woodcock offer fine sport too, yet I trust shooting oneself would be a nobler kind of hunting.

before: How long will we sit on porches practising stale, idle virtues that any real work would render irrelevant? As though one began a day in long-suffering while hiring someone to hoe one’s potatoes, then went out after lunch to practise Christian meekness and charity with goodness aforethought! Consider humanity’s China pride and stagnant self-satisfaction. This generation rather congratulates itself on coming last in an illustrious line. In Boston, London, Paris, and Rome it recalls its ancestry and complacently discusses its progress in art, science, and literature. Behold the Records of the Philosophical Societies, the public Eulogies of _Great Men!_ Good Adam admires his own virtue. “Yes, we have performed great deeds and sung divine songs that will never die”—meaning while _we_ can still remember them. Where are Assyria’s learned societies and great men? What young philosophers and experimenters we are! Not a single reader of mine has yet lived an entire human life. Perhaps these are merely spring months in our race’s lifetime. We may have had the seven-years’ itch, but Concord has yet to see the seventeen-year locust. We know only a thin skin of our globe. Most people have neither dug six feet down nor leaped that far up. We do not know where we are. Besides, nearly half our time we sleep soundly. Yet we consider ourselves wise and have established an order on the surface. Truly we think deeply and aspire high! Standing above an insect crawling among forest-floor pine needles, trying to hide from me, I wonder why it clings to such humble thoughts. Why hide its head from someone who might benefit it and give its race encouraging news? Then I remember the greater Benefactor and Intelligence above me, the human insect.

before: Newness streams into the world without pause, yet we put up with unbelievable dulness. I need only mention the sermons still heard in the most enlightened countries. Words like joy and sorrow become merely a psalm’s refrain, sung through the nose, while our faith stays with the ordinary and mean. We think only our clothes can change. People call the British Empire great and respectable, the United States a first-rate power. We cannot believe that behind each person a tide rises and falls strong enough to float that empire like a wood chip, if he ever admitted it into his mind. Who knows what seventeen-year locust will emerge next? The government of my world was not devised, like Britain’s, in after-dinner talk over wine.
